name: Belinski-Zakharov Gravitational Solitons
description: Exact vacuum solutions made by the inverse scattering method of Vladimir Belinski and Vladimir Zakharov, which adds solitons to a known solution by algebra alone. Their wave of two solitons on a Kasner universe that expands alike in two directions is two pulses of gravitational wave, which leave the singularity as one and run apart along the light cone.
convention: The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: A splash in a canal spreads out and dies away, and a soliton is the wave that keeps its shape, one hump running on alone [gardner1967]. The way to solve for such waves exactly, any number of humps at once, dates from 1967 and from Clifford Gardner, John Greene, Martin Kruskal, and Robert Miura, who did it for the Korteweg-de Vries equation [gardner1967]. Could Einstein's equations be solved the same way? By 1972 Robert Geroch suspected so: he conjectured that a vacuum spacetime with two commuting symmetries has an infinite group of hidden ones, enough to reach every such solution from flat space [geroch1972, alekseev2010]. The hope reached a title in 1978, Dieter Maison's "Are the stationary, axially symmetric Einstein equations completely integrable?" [maison1978].¶Vladimir Belinski and Vladimir Zakharov answered from the Landau Institute in Moscow with a paper submitted on 13 July 1978, "Integration of the Einstein equations by means of the inverse scattering problem technique and construction of exact soliton solutions" [belinskii1978]. They took a vacuum metric that depends on a time $t$ and one direction $z$ alone, $$ds^2 = f\left(-c^2dt^2 + dz^2\right) + g_{ab}\,dx^a dx^b,$$ a form that with its stationary twin holds plane and cylindrical waves, Robert Gowdy's closed universes, and the black holes of Schwarzschild and Kerr [belinskii1978, gowdy1971]. The equations for the matrix $g_{ab}$ are nonlinear, and Belinski and Zakharov traded them for linear ones: Einstein's equations hold exactly when two linear equations, which carry a free complex number $\lambda$, have a common solution [belinskii1978]. Start from a known solution, the seed, and dress it with a matrix that has poles in $\lambda$, and each pole adds one soliton to the seed by algebra alone [belinskii1978]. The poles move from event to event, $\mu = w - z - \sqrt{(w - z)^2 - c^2t^2}$ with $w$ a constant, and Belinski and Zakharov called them "floating" [belinskii1978].¶Their first seed was Kasner's universe, and where two of its directions expand alike a complex conjugate pair of poles makes a wave [belinskii1978]. They wrote that it "describes the interaction of two localized disturbances": late on, each component of $g_{ab}$ has two extrema in $z$, sitting near the light cone $z^2 = c^2t^2$ [belinskii1978]. Run the film backward and the two humps close in and grow [belinskii1978]. At the singularity $t = 0$ the humps of $g_{11}$ and $g_{22}$ fuse into one, and those of $g_{12}$ stop a distance $2w_2$ apart, twice the imaginary part of $w$ [belinskii1978]. A single real pole makes a hump that outruns light, a solution that in their words "cannot be called solitonic in the strict sense" [belinskii1978].¶Trade the time for a second direction of space, so that nothing moves, and take flat space for the seed [belinskii1979]. Two solitons then make the Kerr-NUT solution, which holds Kerr's rotating black hole [belinskii1978, belinskii1979]. A pair of real poles gives the hole with its horizons, and a complex conjugate pair gives a spin too large for any horizon, a bare singularity [belinskii1979]. Switch the rotation off and the two solitons are Schwarzschild's black hole, and $n$ of them look from far away like $n/2$ bodies strung along the axis, each with a mass of its own [belinskii1979]. B. Kent Harrison found a Bäcklund transformation for the same equations later in 1978 and Gernot Neugebauer another in 1979, and Neugebauer's turned out to coincide with the soliton transformations [harrison1978, neugebauer1979, alekseev2010]. Dietrich Kramer and Neugebauer used it in 1980 to set two Kerr black holes on one axis [kramer1980].¶Do these waves behave as solitons do? Belinski and Daniele Fargion set a pair of them on an anisotropic Kasner universe in 1980 and saw in it "one of the possible mechanisms of creation of gravitational waves due to the initial inhomogeneity of the Universe" [belinsky1980]. Bernard Carr and Enric Verdaguer followed such solutions through time three years later: early on they look like lumps moving at nearly the speed of light, "gravisolitons", and late on like gravitational waves on the expanding background [carr1983]. The same year J. Ibañez and Verdaguer collided two solitons out of four and found the spacetime after the collision "highly distorted", though "null rays do not focus to a singularity" [ibanez1983]. Patricia Boyd, Joan Centrella, and Scott Klasky compared those four solitons with the solitons of the Korteweg-de Vries and sine-Gordon equations in 1991, and reported that the gravitational ones "do not suffer a time delay and behave generally like linear waves under collisions" [boyd1991].¶Belinski and Verdaguer gathered the soliton solutions into a book in 2001: inhomogeneous cosmologies, cylindrical waves, colliding plane waves, and the black holes of Schwarzschild and Kerr [belinski2001]. Andrei Pomeransky carried the method in 2005 to $D$ dimensions with $D - 2$ commuting Killing vectors, and derived the Myers-Perry black hole of five dimensions as two solitons [pomeransky2006]. Henriette Elvang and Pau Figueras used it in 2007 to set a black ring turning in balance around a black hole, the black Saturn [elvang2007].

related.text: The seed. With no soliton added, $P = 0$, $Q = 0$, and $f = \sqrt{w/ct}$, the metric is the Kasner universe that expands alike along $x$ and $y$ [belinskii1978].

The same two Killing vectors and the same field equations, with the direction the waves travel along closed into a circle. Belinski and Zakharov counted Gowdy's closed universes among the solutions their form of the metric holds [belinskii1978, gowdy1971].

Trade the time for a second direction of space and add two solitons to flat space, and the result is the Kerr-NUT solution. Kerr's black hole is the one with two real poles and no NUT parameter [belinskii1979].
Two stationary solitons on flat space, in full. Real poles give the solution with horizons and a complex conjugate pair the one with none [belinskii1979].
Two stationary solitons on flat space with the rotation switched off [belinskii1979].
Two Kerr black holes on one axis, built by Neugebauer's Bäcklund transformations, which coincide with Belinski and Zakharov's soliton transformations [kramer1980, alekseev2010].
Reverse the sign of $f$ and $t$ becomes a radius and $z$ the time. One soliton on a flat seed is then a cylindrical solitary wave that runs in to the axis and is reflected from it [belinskii1978].
The same method in five dimensions. Elvang and Figueras took solitons out of a static seed and put them back turned, and got a black ring in balance around a black hole [elvang2007].
Pomeransky derived the Myers-Perry black hole of five dimensions as two solitons, his test of the method in $D$ dimensions with $D - 2$ commuting Killing vectors [pomeransky2006].

coordinates.name: Pole Coordinates

parameters.description: Length that sets the scale ($w > 0$), the imaginary part of the constant in Belinski and Zakharov's pole trajectory
Dimensionless, with $\cosh\beta$ and $\sinh\beta$ the two constants of Belinski and Zakharov whose squares differ by one; at $\beta = 0$ the metric is diagonal and the wave has one polarisation
Dimensionless function of $\tau$ and $\xi$, positive at every event

coordinates.convention: We use the coordinates $(\tau, \xi, x, y)$ in which Belinski and Zakharov's pole trajectories are elementary, with $\tau$ the time and $\xi$ along the direction the waves travel, both pure numbers, and $x$ and $y$ lengths along the two Killing vectors. The length $w$ carries the scale, so no factor of $c$ appears. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Belinski and Zakharov's Chart

parameters.description: Dimensionless function of $t$ and $z$; in a vacuum $\partial_t\ln f = -\dfrac{1}{2ct} + \dfrac{ct}{2}\left(\left(\partial_tP\right)^2 + \left(\partial_zP\right)^2 + e^{2P}\left(\left(\partial_tQ\right)^2 + \left(\partial_zQ\right)^2\right)\right)$ and $\partial_z\ln f = ct\left(\partial_tP\,\partial_zP + e^{2P}\partial_tQ\,\partial_zQ\right)$, with $\partial_t$ the derivative along $ct$

Wave amplitude, a dimensionless function of $t$ and $z$; the spacetime is a vacuum exactly where $\partial_t^2P + \dfrac{1}{ct}\partial_tP - \partial_z^2P = e^{2P}\left(\left(\partial_tQ\right)^2 - \left(\partial_zQ\right)^2\right)$ together with the equations for $Q$ and $f$

Twist of the two polarisations, a dimensionless function of $t$ and $z$, with $Q = 0$ the diagonal case; in a vacuum $\partial_t^2Q + \dfrac{1}{ct}\partial_tQ - \partial_z^2Q = -2\left(\partial_tP\,\partial_tQ - \partial_zP\,\partial_zQ\right)$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, z, x, y)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, $z$ a length along the direction the waves travel, and $x$ and $y$ lengths along the two Killing vectors. The functions $f$, $P$, and $Q$ stand free in every component, and no component assumes a field equation. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, so $\partial_t$ of a function is its derivative along $ct$ and $\dot{t}$ in the geodesic equations means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
